comments.why: Short flight through an ASML High-NA machine showing why competing is hard.
comments.text: LOL, I recommend highly to everyone who thinks a startup can challenge ASML this 1.38min video: [VIDEO] Its an industrial flight video through a ASML TWIN Exe HighNAV. Here is also a presentation of ~45min at CCC / Germany (in English language) which I highly recommend to watch: [LINK] Especially the explanation how they use two milisecond laser shots to first molt the tin and then distribute it symetrically(!!!) with a second shot across the surface. There IS NO chance that this startup will be able to somehow compete, if even Chinese state actors cant do it (yet).

comments.author: danparsonson
comments.story: Dutch Align with US Export Controls on Some ASML Chip Tools
comments.text: The rest of the machine is no less incredible - the EUV light is reflected off a series of mirrors (the largest weighing, IIRC, somewhere in the region of 300kg, and the largest that Zeiss have ever made) onto a mask of the target pattern, which is rapidly shuttling back and forth, onto another series of mirrors, and finally focused onto the wafer stage, which is also moving precisely in step with the mask, to expose the photoresist on a single die which is on the order of 10mm square. And each wafer goes through multiple cycles of this, so not only does the machine rapidly create features at the nanonmetre scale with incredible accuracy, but again and again in exactly the same place after removing and returning the wafer. Oh, and the wafer stage is pretty fun too; it uses an electrostatic chuck that induces a charge in the wafer and therefore holds it firmly in place without needing any kind of suction that could distort the wafer. Promotional fly through video from ASML here: [VIDEO] Asianometry video about the stage: [LINK] Another short video about the light source: [LINK]

comments.author: danparsonson
comments.why: Promotional render of the real EUV machine.
comments.text: Fly-through promotional render of the real thing: [VIDEO] Incredible technology - the light-source works by generating droplets of molten tin, firing them through a chamber at around (IIRC) 200mph, and hitting each droplet with two laser pulses... at 50kHz. How they achieve that using Lego is beyond me.
